title: Νεανίσκοι καὶ μάγειρος
titleEn: The Young Men and the Butcher
part: The Young Men and the Butcher (Chambry 246 · Perry 66)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 246 (= Perry 66). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Δύο νεανίσκοι ἐν ταὐτῷ κρέας ὠνοῦντο.
sentences.tr: Dyo neaniskoi en tautōi kreas ōnounto.
sentences.l: Two young men were buying meat in the same place.
sentences.n: ταὐτῷ is τῷ αὐτῷ run together by crasis, and ἐν ταὐτῷ is the ordinary phrase for 'in one and the same place' — the two are at the same counter at the same moment. The μάγειρος of the next line is butcher, sacrificer and cook in a single Greek word; where he is at the fire the corpus calls him a cook (178, 183), and here, where he is selling the meat, a butcher.

sentences.t: Καὶ δὴ τοῦ μαγείρου περισπασθέντος, ὁ ἕτερος ὑφελόμενος ἀκροκώλιον, εἰς τὸν τοῦ ἑτέρου κόλπον καθῆκεν.
sentences.tr: Kai dē tou mageirou perispasthentos, ho heteros hyphelomenos akrokōlion, eis ton tou heterou kolpon kathēken.
sentences.l: And so, the butcher having been drawn off, the one of them, having filched a trotter, let it down into the other's bosom.
sentences.n: A genitive absolute sets up the theft; περισπάω is to pull a man round and away from what he was attending to. ἀκροκώλιον is the extremity of the beast — foot or trotter, the cheap piece. κόλπος is the fold of the cloak over the breast, where a Greek carried whatever his hands were too full for; putting the meat there makes the second man the one who has it.

sentences.t: Ἐπιστραφέντος δὲ αὐτοῦ καὶ ἐπιζητοῦντος, αἰτιωμένου τε ἐκείνους, ὁ μὲν εἰληφὼς ὤμνυε μὴ ἔχειν, ὁ δὲ ἔχων μὴ εἰληφέναι.
sentences.tr: Epistraphentos de autou kai epizētountos, aitiōmenou te ekeinous, ho men eilēphōs ōmnye mē echein, ho de echōn mē eilēphenai.
sentences.l: And he having turned about and being in search of it, and accusing them, the one who had taken it swore that he did not have it, and the one who had it, that he had not taken it.
sentences.i: And when the man turned round, went looking for it and charged them with the theft, the one who had taken it swore he did not have it, and the one who had it swore he had not taken it.
sentences.n: The chiasmus is the point: taker and holder are different men, so each can swear something that is true as far as the words go. εἰληφώς is the perfect participle of λαμβάνω and εἰληφέναι its infinitive — the perfect because what is at issue is the state left behind by the taking. μή, not οὐ, is the regular negative with an infinitive after ὄμνυμι.

sentences.t: Καὶ ὁ μάγειρος αἰσθόμενος αὐτῶν τὴν κακοτεχνίαν, εἶπεν· « Ἀλλὰ κἂν ἐμὲ λάθητε ἐπιορκοῦντες, θεοὺς μέντοι γε οὐ λήσετε. »
sentences.tr: Kai ho mageiros aisthomenos autōn tēn kakotechnian, eipen· « Alla kan eme lathēte epiorkountes, theous mentoi ge ou lēsete. »
sentences.l: And the butcher, having perceived their trickery, said: « Well, even if you escape me in swearing falsely, the gods at any rate you will not escape. »
sentences.n: λανθάνω with a supplementary participle works the opposite way round from English: ἐπιορκοῦντες carries the deed and the verb says only that it went unseen — 'you may get away with perjuring yourselves so far as I am concerned'. The person kept in the dark stands in the accusative (ἐμέ, θεούς), and the two are set against each other by μέντοι γε. κἄν is again καὶ ἐάν by crasis, with the subjunctive λάθητε.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι ἡ αὐτή ἐστιν ἡ ἀσέβεια τῆς ἐπιορκίας, κἂν αὐτήν τις κατασοφίζηται.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti hē autē estin hē asebeia tēs epiorkias, kan autēn tis katasophizētai.
sentences.l: The story shows that the impiety of perjury is the same, even if someone outwits it by sophistry.
sentences.n: κατασοφίζομαι is to get the better of a thing by cleverness — here the neat division of one lie between two mouths, so that neither says a false word. ἡ αὐτή stands as predicate: the impiety is the same impiety, whatever contrivance is laid over it. A false oath was an offence against the gods invoked, not against the man deceived, which is why the butcher's threat is the one that lands.
